error_modes.label: Course deviation from the assigned radial

texts.0: SP, due to a correction started only after the CDI had already moved well off centre, did not stop the deviation from the assigned radial. Course error exceeded 8 deg and kept increasing, with the aircraft crossing the course a second time before any adequate heading was flown. IP intervened and directed the heading required to regain the assigned radial.
texts.1: SP, due to corrections sized without regard to the drift already present, did not arrest the deviation from the assigned radial. Course error reached 8 deg and stayed at that value until the IP prompted verbally. SP then regained the course, but the recovery followed the prompt and was not initiated by SP.
texts.2: SP, due to late recognition of the CDI trend, did not begin the correction at the first indication of drift off the assigned radial. Course error reached 7 deg before an adequate intercept heading was applied. SP recognized the deviation and returned inside 5 deg in good time and without IP intervention.
texts.3: SP maintained the assigned radial within 5 deg throughout the intercept and the tracking that followed. Corrections were applied at the first CDI movement and were sized so that the course was regained without overshoot.
texts.4: SP held the assigned radial with the CDI centred, with deviations not exceeding 1 to 2 deg at any point of the intercept. Each correction was anticipated from the rate of needle movement rather than from its displacement, so the course was flown with no visible needle excursion.
texts.marginal: SP kept the course deviation inside the 5 deg standard, but the CDI was repeatedly allowed to reach about 4 deg before a correction was applied. The corrections were triggered by displacement rather than by trend, which left a thin margin to the standard on the outbound leg. SP is expected to correct at the first needle movement so that the deviation stays within 2 to 3 deg.

texts_at.0: SP tracked the assigned radial with the IP flying the first corrections and talking through the CDI indications as the exercise began. This is SP's first exposure to the course intercept, and reading the CDI trend rather than its displacement has not yet become a habit. The Training Section introduces this maneuver at this point and does not yet ask for an independent standard. SP is expected to begin reading the CDI trend independently, with the IP available to confirm the picture.
texts_at.1: SP tracked the assigned radial on a stage where code 1 is the expected standard, letting the deviation ride out to about 8 deg, at the outer edge of the tolerance, before turning back toward the course. The correction followed a verbal prompt from the IP rather than SP's own reading of the CDI, because the needle trend is still being noticed only once it is already large. Performance met the desired standard for this stage. SP is expected to pick up the CDI trend earlier so the correction starts before the deviation reaches the edge of the band.
texts_at.2: SP corrected every drift off the assigned radial without prompting, letting the deviation reach about 7 deg before the correction closed the CDI back to centre. The correction is still triggered by how far the needle has moved rather than by the rate at which it is moving. This is consistent with the expected proficiency for the Training Section. SP is expected to begin the correction from the rate of needle movement rather than waiting for a set displacement.
texts_at.3: SP held the assigned radial within 5 deg on three of the four legs flown, applying each correction at the first CDI movement. The fourth leg opened to the full 5 deg before the correction closed it, a single early intercept rather than a recurring pattern. The standard for the Training Section was met. SP is expected to bring the fourth leg into line with the other three so the accuracy is uniform across the exercise.

texts_above.1: SP tracked the assigned radial through the intercept, holding the deviation to about 8 deg, at the tolerance limit, before turning back onto the course. The correction followed a verbal call from the IP. This is above the level the Training Section requires at this point.
texts_above.2: SP corrected every drift off the assigned radial without prompting, holding the peak deviation to about 7 deg before closing it back inside 5 deg in good time. Triggering the correction from the rate of needle movement rather than its displacement would tighten that margin further. The result is above the code required for this Training Section, due to sound course-tracking discipline.
texts_above.3: SP held the assigned radial within 5 deg throughout the intercept and the tracking that followed, applying each correction at the first CDI movement so the course was regained without overshoot. Performance was above the level required at this point of the syllabus, due to very good instrument cross-check.
texts_above.4: SP held the assigned radial with the CDI centred, with deviations not exceeding 1 to 2 deg at any point of the intercept. Each correction was anticipated from the rate of needle movement rather than from its displacement, so the course was flown with no visible needle excursion. This is beyond what the Training Section asks for at this stage, due to outstanding anticipation of drift.

error_modes.label: Solution of the intercept problem and choice of intercept angle

texts.0: SP, due to an incomplete mental model of the intercept sequence that was not updated when the clearance changed, did not solve the problem of the course intercept according to the standardized procedures of AFMAN 11-202 VOL3. SP turned in the wrong direction for the assigned radial and established a heading that diverged from the course. Deviation opened past 8 deg and IP intervened to set the correct intercept heading.
texts.1: SP, due to an aircraft state that had diverged from the SP's mental model without being reassessed, did not determine the required intercept angle before starting the turn. The angle selected was too small for the displacement and the deviation held at 8 deg with no closure on the course. SP revised the angle only after the IP identified the error verbally.
texts.2: SP, due to retention of the briefed mental model after the assigned radial had been changed, did not compute the intercept from the current position relative to the course. The first intercept heading was in error and the deviation grew to 7 deg. SP reassessed the geometry, selected an adequate angle and regained the course inside 5 deg without IP intervention.
texts.3: SP solved the intercept problem correctly, determining the direction of turn and the intercept angle from the current position relative to the assigned course, in accordance with the standardized procedures. The selected angle brought the aircraft onto the course without overshoot and without any prompt from the IP.
texts.4: SP solved the intercept problem immediately and without hesitation, matching the intercept angle to both the displacement and the closure rate. The solution was stated before the turn, required no revision on any of the intercepts, and the course was joined with the CDI centred.
texts.marginal: SP solved the intercept problem correctly, but only after a pause during which the aircraft continued away from the assigned course. No deviation exceeded the standard, yet each solution was reached late enough that a larger intercept angle was then needed to recover the displacement. SP is expected to determine the direction of turn and the intercept angle before the displacement grows.

texts_at.0: SP worked through the intercept problem with the IP talking through the direction of turn and the intercept angle before each turn was started. This is SP's first attempt at building a mental model of the intercept geometry, and relating the current position to the assigned course has not yet become an independent step. This is the level of assistance the Training Section still provides at this stage. SP is expected to begin proposing the direction of turn and the intercept angle, with the IP available to confirm the solution.
texts_at.1: SP solved the intercept problem to the standard expected at this stage, selecting an angle that held the deviation at about 8 deg, at the outer edge of the tolerance. The angle was revised only once the IP identified that the aircraft state no longer matched the picture SP was working from. Performance met the desired standard for this stage. SP is expected to reassess the geometry against the current position rather than the one briefed before the turn.
texts_at.2: SP solved the intercept problem correctly on every leg without prompting, with the deviation reaching about 7 deg before the chosen angle brought the course back. The first solution is still built from the assigned radial rather than the current displacement relative to it. This is consistent with the expected proficiency for the Training Section. SP is expected to base the first intercept angle on the displacement actually observed rather than the nominal one.
texts_at.3: SP solved the intercept problem correctly on three of the four legs, joining the course within 5 deg each time. The remaining leg needed a brief pause to reconcile the geometry after a late course change, rather than any error in the method itself. The maneuver was flown to the standard the Training Section requires at this point. SP is expected to reassess the geometry as soon as a change is issued so no leg needs that pause.

texts_above.1: SP solved the intercept problem, selecting an angle that held the deviation to about 8 deg, at the tolerance limit, before the course was regained. The correction followed a verbal call from the IP. The result is above the code required for this Training Section at this stage of training.
texts_above.2: SP solved the intercept problem correctly on every leg without prompting, with the deviation reaching about 7 deg before the selected angle closed the course back inside 5 deg. Basing the first angle on the observed displacement rather than the nominal one would remove even that peak. The result is above the code required for this Training Section, due to solid navigational problem-solving.
texts_above.3: SP solved the intercept problem correctly on every leg, determining direction and angle from the current position relative to the course and joining it within 5 deg without a prompt. Performance was above the level required at this point of the syllabus, due to sure-handed intercept planning.
texts_above.4: SP solved the intercept problem immediately and without hesitation on every leg, matching the intercept angle to both the displacement and the closure rate and joining the course with the CDI centred. This is beyond what the Training Section asks for at this stage, due to exceptional geometry judgment.

error_modes.label: Lead point and rollout onto the course

texts.0: SP, due to a high intercept angle flown with no lead computed for the closure rate, did not use the appropriate lead when rolling out on the assigned course. SP flew through the course and reached a deviation beyond 8 deg on the opposite side. IP intervened and directed the turn back to the assigned radial.
texts.1: SP, due to a lead taken from the CDI centring instead of from the closure rate, did not start the rollout in time on the assigned course. The overshoot reached 8 deg before any correction began, and the correction started only after the IP called the overshoot. SP then re-intercepted, but the recovery followed the prompt rather than SP's own assessment.
texts.2: SP, due to an underestimated closure rate on a 45 deg intercept, did not apply the appropriate lead when joining the assigned course. The overshoot reached 7 deg on the far side of the course. SP recognized it at once, re-intercepted and settled inside 5 deg without IP intervention.
texts.3: SP used the appropriate lead for the intercept angle and closure rate flown, beginning the rollout so that the aircraft settled on the assigned course within 5 deg. No overshoot required a second intercept and no prompting was needed.
texts.4: SP judged the lead precisely at every intercept angle flown, rolling out so that the CDI centred as the wings came level. The course was joined without overshoot and without any subsequent correction on any of the intercepts.
texts.marginal: SP used a lead that placed the aircraft on course within the standard, but the rollout consistently ended 3 to 4 deg on the far side before the course settled. The rollout was started late at the higher intercept angles. SP is expected to scale the lead with the closure rate so that the course is joined without crossing it.

texts_at.0: SP flew the rollout onto the course with the IP calling the lead point and confirming when to start rolling out on each intercept. This is SP's first exposure to judging lead from the closure rate, and the picture of when to begin the rollout has not yet been built. The maneuver is being introduced at this point of the syllabus, so no independent standard is required yet. SP is expected to begin judging the lead point independently, with the IP available to confirm the call.
texts_at.1: SP used the lead available at this stage to rejoin the course, with the overshoot reaching about 8 deg, at the outer edge of the tolerance, before the aircraft settled. The lead applied was taken from the CDI centring rather than the closure rate, and the second correction followed the IP's prompt. Performance met the desired standard for this stage. SP is expected to judge the lead from the closure rate so the rollout needs fewer follow-up corrections.
texts_at.2: SP applied a workable lead on every intercept without prompting, with the overshoot reaching about 7 deg before the re-intercept closed it. The lead is still sized from the intercept angle alone rather than the closure rate that angle produces. This is consistent with the expected proficiency for the Training Section. SP is expected to size the lead from the actual closure rate observed on each intercept.
texts_at.3: SP used the appropriate lead on three of the four intercepts, rolling out on the assigned course within 5 deg without a second correction. The fourth intercept, flown at a higher angle, needed a small adjustment after rollout rather than a change in method. The standard for the Training Section was met. SP is expected to scale the lead consistently at the higher intercept angles as well as the shallow ones.

texts_above.1: SP judged the lead available at this stage, holding the overshoot to about 8 deg, at the tolerance limit, before the aircraft settled on the course. The correction followed a verbal call from the IP. Performance was above the level required at this point of the syllabus.
texts_above.2: SP applied a workable lead on every intercept without prompting, holding the overshoot to about 7 deg before closing it back inside 5 deg. Sizing the lead from the closure rate rather than the intercept angle alone would remove most of that overshoot. The result is above the code required for this Training Section, due to steady lead-point judgment.
texts_above.3: SP used the appropriate lead for the intercept angle and closure rate on every leg, rolling out within 5 deg with no overshoot requiring a second intercept. Performance was above the level required at this point of the syllabus, due to consistently accurate rollout timing.
texts_above.4: SP judged the lead precisely at every intercept angle flown, rolling out so the CDI centred as the wings came level with no subsequent correction on any intercept. This is beyond what the Training Section asks for at this stage, due to exemplary closure-rate anticipation.

error_modes.label: Inbound and outbound tracking and wind correction

texts.0: SP, due to a wind correction angle that was never established after the course was joined, did not execute the inbound and outbound tracking timely and correctly. Drift accumulated on both legs and the deviation passed 8 deg without any heading change. IP intervened and set the heading required to hold the assigned course.
texts.1: SP, due to corrections applied in fixed increments without bracketing the drift, did not track the assigned radial correctly. The deviation stabilized at 8 deg with no wind correction angle established. SP bracketed the drift and regained the course only after verbal direction from the IP.
texts.2: SP, due to a wind correction angle carried over unchanged from the inbound to the outbound leg, did not adjust the heading for the reversed drift after the course reversal. The deviation opened to 6 deg outbound. SP recognized the trend, bracketed the drift and regained the course inside 5 deg without prompting.
texts.3: SP executed the inbound and outbound tracking timely and correctly, establishing a wind correction angle that held the deviation within 5 deg on both legs. Corrections were bracketed and reduced in size as the drift was identified.
texts.4: SP established the wind correction angle within the first seconds of each leg and held the assigned course with the CDI centred inbound and outbound. Drift was identified from the rate of needle movement and corrected before any measurable displacement developed.
texts.marginal: SP tracked the course inbound and outbound within the standard, but the wind correction angle was found by repeated symmetric corrections rather than by bracketing, leaving a slow oscillation of about 4 deg either side of the course. Tracking accuracy is met but not consolidated, particularly on the outbound leg. SP is expected to bracket the drift and settle on a single wind correction angle.

texts_at.0: SP tracked the inbound and outbound legs with the IP calling the wind correction angle needed and talking through the bracketing on each leg. This is SP's first exposure to bracketing drift on both legs of a course reversal, and settling on a single wind correction angle has not yet become routine. Performance is consistent with a first exposure at this point of the syllabus, where the Training Section still provides assistance. SP is expected to begin bracketing the drift independently, with the IP available to confirm the correction angle.
texts_at.1: SP tracked the inbound and outbound radials to the standard expected at this stage, with the deviation reaching about 8 deg before the drift was corrected. The correction followed the IP's identification of the trend rather than a wind correction angle established beforehand. Performance met the desired standard for this stage. SP is expected to establish a wind correction angle at rollout rather than tracking without one until the drift is called.
texts_at.2: SP tracked both legs without prompting, letting the deviation open to about 6 deg before the wind correction angle closed it. The correction angle is still being adjusted after the course reversal rather than reassessed for the new leg from the outset. This is consistent with the expected proficiency for the Training Section. SP is expected to reassess the wind correction angle as soon as the course reverses rather than carrying the previous value forward.
texts_at.3: SP executed the inbound and outbound tracking correctly, holding the deviation within 5 deg on both legs with corrections bracketed and reduced as the drift was identified. One correction on the outbound leg was slightly larger than the others without affecting the result. The result is in line with the proficiency expected at this point of the syllabus. SP is expected to make the outbound bracketing as consistent as the inbound.

texts_above.1: SP tracked the inbound and outbound legs, holding the deviation to about 8 deg, at the tolerance limit, before the wind correction angle brought the course back. The correction followed a verbal call from the IP. This is beyond what the Training Section asks for at this stage of training.
texts_above.2: SP tracked both legs without prompting, letting the deviation open to about 6 deg before the wind correction angle brought it back inside 5 deg. Reassessing the correction angle at the course reversal, rather than carrying the previous value forward, would remove most of that opening. The result is above the code required for this Training Section, due to dependable wind-correction technique.
texts_above.3: SP executed the inbound and outbound tracking timely and correctly, establishing a wind correction angle that held the deviation within 5 deg on both legs with corrections bracketed and reduced as the drift was identified. Performance was above the level required at this point of the syllabus, due to notably good drift management.
texts_above.4: SP established the wind correction angle within the first seconds of each leg and held the assigned course with the CDI centred inbound and outbound, correcting drift before any measurable displacement developed. This is beyond what the Training Section asks for at this stage, due to superior anticipation of wind effect.

error_modes.label: Station passage and immediate outbound re-intercept

texts.0: SP, due to loss of situational awareness of the aircraft's position relative to the station, did not identify station passage from the TO/FROM reversal and the CDI behavior. SP chased the reversing needle instead of holding the computed outbound heading, and the course error exceeded 8 deg once the area of unreliable indications was left behind. IP intervened and re-established the outbound course.
texts.1: SP, due to degraded situational awareness after the change of sequence at the station, did not hold the computed heading through the area of CDI unreliability at station passage. The needle was chased throughout the passage and the deviation stood at 8 deg after the station. SP set the correct outbound heading only after the IP identified station passage verbally.
texts.2: SP, due to situational awareness limited to the instrument in use at the moment of station passage, did not start the outbound intercept immediately after the TO/FROM reversal. The delay allowed the deviation to reach 6 deg on the outbound radial. SP then recognized the passage, applied an adequate intercept angle and regained the course without IP intervention.
texts.3: SP identified station passage from the TO/FROM reversal, held the computed heading through the unreliable indications, then intercepted the outbound radial immediately and tracked it within 5 deg. No prompting was required at any point of the passage.
texts.4: SP anticipated station passage, held the outbound heading through the unreliable CDI indications without a single correction, and re-established the outbound course with the needle centred as soon as the indications settled. The transition from inbound to outbound was continuous, with no measurable deviation.
texts.marginal: SP handled the intercept immediately after station passage within the standard, but reacted to the first CDI fluctuations before the passage was confirmed, and the outbound course was re-established with about 4 deg of deviation. The technique depends on catching the reversal late rather than anticipating it. SP is expected to hold the computed heading through the area of unreliable indications and to start the outbound intercept at the confirmed passage.

texts_at.0: SP flew through station passage with the IP calling the TO/FROM reversal and talking through the outbound intercept heading as the indications settled. This is SP's first exposure to the area of CDI unreliability at station passage, and holding the computed heading through it rather than chasing the needle has not yet been built. The Training Section still expects IP assistance for this maneuver at this point. SP is expected to begin holding the computed heading through the passage independently, with the IP available to confirm the reversal.
texts_at.1: SP handled station passage to the standard expected at this stage, with the deviation reaching about 8 deg after the reversal before the outbound course was regained. The outbound heading was set only after the IP identified station passage verbally, because the needle was still being chased through the area of unreliable indications. Performance met the desired standard for this stage. SP is expected to hold the computed heading through the passage rather than reacting to the needle while it is unreliable.
texts_at.2: SP recognized station passage on every leg without prompting, with the deviation reaching about 6 deg on the outbound radial before the intercept closed it. The outbound intercept is still started a moment after the reversal rather than anticipated before it. This is consistent with the expected proficiency for the Training Section. SP is expected to anticipate the reversal so the outbound intercept begins as the passage is confirmed rather than just after it.
texts_at.3: SP identified station passage and intercepted the outbound radial within 5 deg on three of the four passages without a prompt. The remaining passage needed a brief extra check of the TO/FROM indication before the intercept began, rather than any error in the sequence used. This is consistent with the expected proficiency for the Training Section. SP is expected to make that check as quick on every passage as it was on the other three.

texts_above.1: SP handled station passage, holding the deviation after the reversal to about 8 deg, at the tolerance limit, before the outbound course was regained. The correction followed a verbal call from the IP. This is above the level the Training Section requires at this point.
texts_above.2: SP recognized station passage on every leg without prompting, holding the deviation to about 6 deg on the outbound radial before the intercept closed it inside 5 deg. Starting the outbound intercept at the confirmed passage, rather than a moment after it, would tighten that margin further. The result is above the code required for this Training Section, due to assured handling of the passage sequence.
texts_above.3: SP identified station passage from the TO/FROM reversal, held the computed heading through the unreliable indications and intercepted the outbound radial within 5 deg on every passage without a prompt. Performance was above the level required at this point of the syllabus, due to precise recognition of the reversal.
texts_above.4: SP anticipated station passage and held the outbound heading through the unreliable CDI indications with no correction, re-establishing the outbound course with the needle centred as the indications settled. This is beyond what the Training Section asks for at this stage, due to first-rate transition technique.

error_modes.label: Navaid tuning, identification and course setting for the intercept

texts.0: SP, due to a course set on the OBS that did not match the assigned radial and a navaid that was never identified, did not establish the correct reference before executing the intercept. The aircraft was flown accurately to a course other than the one assigned, leaving an error far beyond 8 deg from the cleared radial. IP intervened and reset the navigation reference.
texts.1: SP, due to an omitted check of the tuned frequency and identifier before starting the intercept, did not confirm that the displayed course was the assigned one. The intercept was flown against an offset course setting and the error remained at 8 deg from the assigned radial. SP corrected the setting only after the IP called for the identification check.
texts.2: SP, due to setting the OBS after the turn had already been started, did not have the intercept reference established before the maneuver. The initial heading was flown against the previous course setting and the deviation reached 6 deg. SP detected the error from the CDI behavior, reset the course and regained the assigned radial without IP intervention.
texts.3: SP tuned, identified and set the navaid for the assigned course before each intercept, so that every intercept was flown against a verified reference. Course settings matched the assignment throughout and no correction of the setup was required.
texts.4: SP completed the tune, identify and set sequence ahead of every intercept and cross-checked the displayed course against the clearance before turning. The navigation reference was correct on every leg, including the change between VOR/TACAN and GPS OBS mode, with no interruption of the tracking.
texts.marginal: SP set and identified the navaid correctly, but the sequence was completed only just before the turn was required, leaving no margin for a setup error. The setup meets the standard while remaining reactive to the clearance rather than anticipating it. SP is expected to complete tune, identify and set early enough to cross-check the course before the intercept begins.

texts_at.0: SP tuned and set the navaid for the intercept with the IP talking through the identification check and the course setting before each turn. This is SP's first exposure to the tune, identify and set sequence for a course intercept, and completing it ahead of the turn has not yet become a fixed habit. The Training Section introduces this maneuver at this point and does not yet ask for an independent standard. SP is expected to begin completing the setup independently before each turn, with the IP available to confirm the reference.
texts_at.1: SP set up the navaid to the standard expected at this stage, with the deviation reaching about 8 deg before the reference was corrected. The identification check was completed only after the IP called for it, because the OBS is still being set from memory rather than confirmed against the assignment. Performance met the desired standard for this stage. SP is expected to confirm the tuned frequency and identifier before starting the turn rather than after the deviation appears.
texts_at.2: SP set up the navaid correctly before most intercepts without prompting, with the deviation reaching about 6 deg once before the course was reset and regained. The setup on that leg was completed after the turn had already started rather than before it. This is consistent with the expected proficiency for the Training Section. SP is expected to complete tune, identify and set before the turn on every leg, not only most of them.
texts_at.3: SP tuned, identified and set the navaid before three of the four intercepts, flying each against a verified reference within 5 deg. The remaining intercept was flown against a setting confirmed a few seconds into the turn rather than before it, without affecting the result. The result is in line with the proficiency expected at this point of the syllabus. SP is expected to complete the setup before every turn so none are flown against an unconfirmed reference.

texts_above.1: SP set up the navaid for the intercept, holding the deviation to about 8 deg, at the tolerance limit, before the reference was corrected and the course regained. The correction followed a verbal call from the IP. The result is above the code required for this Training Section at this stage of training.
texts_above.2: SP set up the navaid correctly before most intercepts without prompting, with the deviation reaching about 6 deg once before the course was reset and regained inside 5 deg. Completing tune, identify and set before every turn, rather than after most of them, would remove that single excursion. The result is above the code required for this Training Section, due to competent navaid-setup discipline.
texts_above.3: SP tuned, identified and set the navaid for the assigned course before each intercept, so every intercept was flown against a verified reference with course settings matching the assignment throughout. Performance was above the level required at this point of the syllabus, due to disciplined setup sequencing.
texts_above.4: SP completed the tune, identify and set sequence ahead of every intercept and cross-checked the displayed course against the clearance before turning, including the change between VOR/TACAN and GPS OBS mode. This is beyond what the Training Section asks for at this stage, due to faultless navigation-reference management.

error_modes.label: Basic aircraft control while working the intercept

texts.0: SP, due to an attention bottleneck on the course indication at the expense of the instrument cross-check, did not maintain the Basic A/C Control Criteria while flying the intercept. Altitude departed by more than 300 ft and airspeed by more than 20 KIAS during the intercept turn. IP intervened to recover the assigned altitude and airspeed.
texts.1: SP, due to attention captured by the navigation display while the aircraft state went unmonitored, did not hold altitude and heading during the intercept. Altitude reached 300 ft below the assigned level and the rollout heading was 8 deg in error, at the tolerance limit. SP restored both parameters only after the IP called the deviations.
texts.2: SP, due to absorption in the course indication during the intercept turn, did not maintain the Basic A/C Control Criteria at the required standard. Altitude deviated by 250 ft and airspeed by 15 KIAS while the turn was flown. SP resumed the cross-check, corrected both and returned inside 150 ft and 10 KIAS without IP intervention.
texts.3: SP maintained altitude within 150 ft, airspeed within 10 KIAS and heading within 5 deg throughout the intercepts while working the course problem. The instrument cross-check continued through the turns and the navigation task did not displace aircraft control.
texts.4: SP flew the intercepts with altitude, airspeed and heading effectively constant, with deviations not exceeding 50 ft and 5 KIAS. Trim was used so that the aircraft held the parameters while attention was given to the course, and the cross-check remained continuous through every turn.
texts.marginal: SP held the Basic A/C Control Criteria inside the standards, but altitude drifted to about 120 ft during each intercept turn and was recovered only after the turn was completed. The scan narrows towards the navigation display whenever the intercept problem is being solved. SP is expected to keep the cross-check running through the turn so that altitude does not move more than 50 ft.

texts_at.0: SP flew the intercepts with the IP calling the altitude and heading trends and helping keep the cross-check running while the course problem was being worked. This is SP's first exposure to dividing attention between the course problem and the flight instruments, and keeping the cross-check running through the turn has not yet been built. This is the level of assistance the Training Section still provides at this stage. SP is expected to begin bringing the altimeter and heading indicator back into the scan independently during the turn, with the IP available to call any trend that is missed.
texts_at.1: SP held the Basic A/C Control parameters to the standard expected at this stage while working the intercept, with altitude reaching 300 ft below the assigned level and the rollout heading 8 deg in error before both were restored. The correction followed the IP's call rather than SP's own cross-check, because attention is still being held on the navigation display through the turn. Performance met the desired standard for this stage. SP is expected to bring the altimeter and heading indicator back into the scan as the intercept turn is flown.
texts_at.2: SP resumed the cross-check without prompting on every intercept, with altitude deviating by 250 ft and airspeed by 15 KIAS before both were corrected back inside 150 ft and 10 KIAS. The scan is still narrowing toward the course indication for the first part of each turn rather than staying distributed throughout it. This is consistent with the expected proficiency for the Training Section. SP is expected to keep the cross-check running from the start of the turn rather than resuming it partway through.
texts_at.3: SP maintained altitude within 150 ft, airspeed within 10 KIAS and heading within 5 deg through three of the four intercepts while working the course problem. The fourth intercept showed a brief widening of the scan during a busy navaid re-tune rather than any lapse in technique. The result is in line with the proficiency expected at this point of the syllabus. SP is expected to hold the same scan distribution through a busy re-tune as through a straightforward one.

texts_above.1: SP held the Basic A/C Control parameters while working the intercept, containing the altitude excursion to about 300 ft and the rollout heading to about 8 deg, both at the tolerance limit for the stage. The correction followed a verbal call from the IP. Performance was above the level required at this point of the syllabus.
texts_above.2: SP resumed the cross-check without prompting on every intercept, containing altitude to 250 ft and airspeed to 15 KIAS before both were corrected back inside 150 ft and 10 KIAS. Keeping the scan distributed from the start of the turn, rather than resuming it partway through, would shrink those excursions further. The result is above the code required for this Training Section, due to steady instrument cross-check.
texts_above.3: SP maintained altitude within 150 ft, airspeed within 10 KIAS and heading within 5 deg throughout the intercepts while working the course problem, with the cross-check continuing through every turn. Performance was above the level required at this point of the syllabus, due to well-developed scan distribution.
texts_above.4: SP flew the intercepts with altitude, airspeed and heading effectively constant, trimmed so the aircraft held the parameters while attention was given to the course, with the cross-check continuous through every turn. This is beyond what the Training Section asks for at this stage, due to superior division of attention.

error_modes.label: INBOUND INTERCEPT ANGLE AT OR BEYOND THE 90 DEG INDEX

texts.0: SP, due to an inbound intercept heading built with the course arrow below the 90 deg index, did not keep the intercept angle less than 90 deg as the technique requires. The aircraft closed the course almost perpendicular to it, the CDI swung across the case faster than the rollout could absorb and the deviation opened beyond 8 deg on the far side. IP intervened and directed the heading required to regain the assigned radial.
texts.1: SP, due to an intercept angle taken up to the 90 deg index for a displacement that did not call for it, did not limit the inbound intercept angle as the technique requires. Closure could not be judged from the needle rate and the overshoot settled at 8 deg on the opposite side of the course. SP reduced the angle and re-intercepted only after the IP called the excessive intercept angle.
texts.2: SP, due to an inbound intercept angle selected close to the 90 deg index for a small displacement, did not keep the course arrow in the upper half of the case as the technique requires. Closure was faster than the lead allowed and the deviation reached 7 deg past the course. SP recognized the geometry, reduced the intercept angle and settled within 5 deg without IP intervention.
texts.3: SP kept every inbound intercept angle less than 90 deg, with the course arrow above the 90 deg index, and sized the angle to the number of degrees off the selected course. Closure stayed controllable and the assigned radial was joined within 5 deg on each intercept.
texts.4: SP selected inbound intercept angles well inside the 90 deg limit and varied them with both the displacement and the rate of intercept desired. The course arrow stayed high in the case on every intercept, closure was uniform and the radial was joined with deviations not exceeding 1 to 2 deg.
texts.marginal: SP kept the inbound intercept angles below 90 deg, but the course arrow was worked close to the 90 deg index whenever the displacement was large, and the resulting closure left about 4 deg of overshoot before the course settled. The deviation stayed inside the standard, yet the angle is being chosen at the edge of the limit rather than for the rate of intercept desired. SP is expected to keep the course arrow clearly above the 90 deg index so that closure remains controllable at rollout.

texts_at.0: SP flew inbound intercepts with the IP setting the course arrow position and confirming each intercept angle chosen. This is SP's first exposure to limiting the intercept angle by the course arrow position, and judging closure from the angle chosen has not yet been built. The maneuver is being introduced at this point of the syllabus, so no independent standard is required yet. SP is expected to begin keeping the course arrow above the index independently, with the IP available to confirm the angle.
texts_at.1: SP kept the inbound intercept angle close to the 90 deg index at the standard expected at this stage, with the resulting deviation reaching about 8 deg before the course was regained. The angle was reduced only after the IP called the excessive intercept angle, because closure at that angle is still being underestimated. Performance met the desired standard for this stage. SP is expected to judge closure from the intercept angle before it is selected rather than after the overshoot appears.
texts_at.2: SP kept the course arrow in the upper half of the case on every intercept without prompting, with the deviation reaching about 7 deg before the reduced angle closed it. The initial angle is still chosen close to the 90 deg index for displacements that do not require it. This is consistent with the expected proficiency for the Training Section. SP is expected to size the initial angle to the displacement rather than defaulting toward the 90 deg index.
texts_at.3: SP kept every inbound intercept angle below 90 deg and joined the assigned radial within 5 deg on three of the four intercepts. The fourth needed a marginally later rollout at the higher displacement without any change to the technique used. The maneuver was flown to the standard the Training Section requires at this point. SP is expected to hold the same rollout timing at the larger displacements as at the smaller ones.

texts_above.1: SP kept the inbound intercept angle close to the index, holding the resulting deviation to about 8 deg, at the tolerance limit, before the course was regained. The correction followed a verbal call from the IP. This is beyond what the Training Section asks for at this stage of training.
texts_above.2: SP kept the course arrow in the upper half of the case on every intercept without prompting, holding the deviation to about 7 deg before the reduced angle closed it inside 5 deg. Sizing the initial angle to the displacement, rather than defaulting toward the 90 deg index, would remove that peak. The result is above the code required for this Training Section, due to sound intercept-angle judgment.
texts_above.3: SP kept every inbound intercept angle less than 90 deg, with the course arrow above the 90 deg index, sizing the angle to the number of degrees off course so closure stayed controllable and the radial was joined within 5 deg on each intercept. Performance was above the level required at this point of the syllabus, due to very good angle selection.
texts_above.4: SP selected inbound intercept angles well inside the 90 deg limit and varied them with both the displacement and the rate of intercept desired, joining the radial with deviations not exceeding 1 to 2 deg. This is beyond what the Training Section asks for at this stage, due to exceptional closure control.

error_modes.label: TURN IN THE SHORTER DIRECTION TOWARD THE CDI

texts.0: SP, due to a turn started the longer way round instead of in the shorter direction toward the CDI, did not place the head of the course arrow in the top half of the instrument case. The aircraft turned away from the assigned course through more than 180 deg of heading change and the deviation opened past 8 deg while the turn continued. IP intervened and reversed the turn onto a usable intercept heading.
texts.1: SP, due to a direction of turn taken from the heading difference alone instead of from the position of the CDI, did not turn the shorter way toward the needle. The intercept was set up from the wrong side, the deviation stood at 8 deg and showed no closure on the course. SP reversed the turn only after the IP identified the wrong direction verbally.
texts.2: SP, due to a turn begun before the side of the CDI was checked, did not turn in the shorter direction toward the course on the first intercept. The deviation grew to 7 deg during the reversal of the turn. SP identified the error when the head of the course arrow left the top half of the case, reversed the turn and regained the course within 5 deg without IP intervention.
texts.3: SP turned in the shorter direction toward the CDI on every intercept, placing the head of the course arrow in the top half of the instrument case before rolling out on the intercept heading. The direction of turn was correct throughout and the assigned course was joined within 5 deg.
texts.4: SP established the direction of turn from the side of the CDI immediately on each clearance, with no hesitation and no reversal at any point. The head of the course arrow was in the top half of the case from the start of every turn and the course was joined with deviations not exceeding 1 to 2 deg.
texts.marginal: SP turned the shorter way toward the CDI on each intercept, but the direction was confirmed after the bank was already established rather than before it, and one intercept was flown out to about 4 deg while the geometry was checked. Deviations stayed inside the standard while the direction of turn is still being verified late. SP is expected to read the side of the CDI and place the head of the course arrow in the top half of the case before starting the turn.

texts_at.0: SP turned toward the CDI with the IP calling the side of the needle and confirming the direction of turn before each intercept was started. This is SP's first exposure to reading the side of the CDI before committing to a turn, and checking it ahead of the bank has not yet become automatic. Performance is consistent with a first exposure at this point of the syllabus, where the Training Section still provides assistance. SP is expected to begin checking the side of the CDI independently before turning, with the IP available to confirm the direction.
texts_at.1: SP turned toward the CDI at the standard expected at this stage, with the deviation reaching about 8 deg before the direction of turn was corrected. The reversal was made only after the IP identified the wrong direction verbally, because the side of the CDI is still being read from the heading difference rather than the display itself. Performance met the desired standard for this stage. SP is expected to check the side of the CDI before committing to a direction of turn.
texts_at.2: SP turned in the shorter direction toward the CDI on every intercept without prompting, with the deviation reaching about 7 deg during one reversal before the course was regained. The turn is still started a moment before the side of the CDI is confirmed rather than after it. This is consistent with the expected proficiency for the Training Section. SP is expected to confirm the side of the CDI before the bank is applied on every intercept, not only most of them.
texts_at.3: SP turned in the shorter direction toward the CDI on three of the four intercepts, placing the course arrow in the top half of the case before rolling out within 5 deg. The fourth intercept needed a brief check of the display before committing, without any reversal of direction. The result is in line with the proficiency expected at this point of the syllabus. SP is expected to make that check as quick on every intercept as it was on the other three.

texts_above.1: SP turned toward the CDI, holding the resulting deviation to about 8 deg, at the tolerance limit, before the direction of turn was corrected. The correction followed a verbal call from the IP. This is above the level the Training Section requires at this point.
texts_above.2: SP turned in the shorter direction toward the CDI on every intercept without prompting, holding the deviation from one reversal to about 7 deg before closing it inside 5 deg. Confirming the side of the CDI before the bank is applied, on every intercept rather than most, would remove that reversal. The result is above the code required for this Training Section, due to solid turn-direction discipline.
texts_above.3: SP established the direction of turn from the side of the CDI immediately on each clearance, placing the head of the course arrow in the top half of the instrument case before rolling out and joining the assigned course within 5 deg. Performance was above the level required at this point of the syllabus, due to consistently accurate direction sense.
texts_above.4: SP established the direction of turn from the side of the CDI with no hesitation and no reversal at any point, joining the course with deviations not exceeding 1 to 2 deg on every intercept. This is beyond what the Training Section asks for at this stage, due to outstanding read of the CDI presentation.

error_modes.label: TO INDICATION CHECK AFTER SETTING THE INBOUND COURSE

texts.0: SP, due to an omitted check for a TO indication after setting the inbound course, did not confirm that the radial had been converted into an inbound course before starting the intercept. The reciprocal was left in the course window, corrections were flown in the direction opposite to the needle and the deviation ran beyond 8 deg. IP intervened, reset the inbound course and directed the intercept.
texts.1: SP, due to a course set from the radial without checking the TO or FROM indication, did not verify the course reference before the intercept. The CDI was displaced with a FROM indication on an inbound leg, the corrections did not close the course and the deviation held at 8 deg. SP reset the inbound course only after the IP called for the TO check.
texts.2: SP, due to the TO indication being read only after the intercept turn had begun, did not check the course window before starting the intercept. The first correction was applied against a reversed sense and the deviation reached 7 deg. SP caught the FROM indication, reset the inbound course and regained the radial within 5 deg without IP intervention.
texts.3: SP set the inbound course, converting the assigned radial where required, and checked for a TO indication before every intercept. Sensing was correct throughout, corrections closed the course and the deviation stayed within 5 deg.
texts.4: SP converted each assigned radial to the inbound course and confirmed the TO indication as part of the setup, before any turn was started. Sensing was verified on every intercept without prompting and the course was flown with deviations not exceeding 1 to 2 deg.
texts.marginal: SP checked the TO indication on each inbound course, but the check was made only as the turn was rolling in, and on one intercept the sense was confirmed with the CDI already about 4 deg out. The deviations remained inside the standard while verification is still being done after the turn is committed. SP is expected to check for the TO indication immediately after setting the inbound course and before the intercept turn.

texts_at.0: SP set the inbound course with the IP calling for the TO indication check and confirming the sense before the first correction was flown. This is SP's first exposure to verifying the TO indication before correcting, and checking it ahead of the turn has not yet been built into the setup. The Training Section still expects IP assistance for this maneuver at this point. SP is expected to begin checking for the TO indication independently after setting the course, with the IP available to confirm the sense.
texts_at.1: SP checked for a TO indication at the standard expected at this stage, with the deviation reaching about 8 deg before the reversed sense was found and corrected. The inbound course was reset only after the IP called for the TO check, because the indication is still being checked after the correction begins rather than before it. Performance met the desired standard for this stage. SP is expected to check for the TO indication immediately after setting the inbound course and before any correction is flown.
texts_at.2: SP checked the TO indication before most intercepts without prompting, with the deviation reaching about 7 deg once before the reset course was regained. That check is still made after the turn has begun on the leg where the reversed sense appeared. This is consistent with the expected proficiency for the Training Section. SP is expected to make the TO check before every intercept turn, not only most of them.
texts_at.3: SP set the inbound course and checked for a TO indication before three of the four intercepts, holding the deviation within 5 deg each time. The fourth intercept had the check confirmed a moment into the turn rather than before it, without a sensing error resulting. The standard for the Training Section was met. SP is expected to complete the check before every turn so none are started on an unconfirmed sense.

texts_above.1: SP checked for a TO indication, holding the resulting deviation to about 8 deg, at the tolerance limit, before the reversed sense was found and corrected. The correction followed a verbal call from the IP. The result is above the code required for this Training Section at this stage of training.
texts_above.2: SP checked the TO indication before most intercepts without prompting, holding the deviation from the one exception to about 7 deg before the reset course closed inside 5 deg. Making the check before every intercept turn, rather than most of them, would remove that exception. The result is above the code required for this Training Section, due to dependable indication cross-check.
texts_above.3: SP set the inbound course, converting the assigned radial where required, and checked for a TO indication before every intercept, with sensing correct throughout and the deviation staying within 5 deg. Performance was above the level required at this point of the syllabus, due to notably good verification habit.
texts_above.4: SP converted each assigned radial to the inbound course and confirmed the TO indication as part of the setup before any turn was started, with sensing verified on every intercept without prompting. This is beyond what the Training Section asks for at this stage, due to exemplary setup verification.

error_modes.label: CONSTRUCTION OF THE INBOUND INTERCEPT HEADING FROM THE BEARING POINTER

texts.0: SP, due to an inbound intercept heading that was estimated instead of being built from the course arrow to the bearing pointer and 30 deg beyond it, did not determine a heading that would close the assigned course. The heading flown fell short of the bearing pointer, the aircraft paralleled the radial and the deviation stayed beyond 8 deg with no closure. IP intervened and set the correct intercept heading.
texts.1: SP, due to an intercept heading taken to the bearing pointer without continuing 30 deg past it, did not establish an angle that would bring the aircraft onto the assigned course. Closure was negligible and the deviation remained at the 8 deg limit for the whole leg. SP added the required intercept angle only after the IP prompted with the heading to fly.
texts.2: SP, due to the 30 deg increment being applied from the course arrow instead of from the bearing pointer, did not build the inbound intercept heading as the technique describes. The resulting angle was too small for the displacement and the deviation reached 7 deg before closure began. SP rebuilt the heading from the bearing pointer and joined the course within 5 deg without IP intervention.
texts.3: SP built each inbound intercept heading from the course arrow, up the case to the bearing pointer and 30 deg beyond it, and flew that heading until the rollout. The angle produced steady closure and the assigned course was joined within 5 deg on every intercept.
texts.4: SP produced the inbound intercept heading immediately on each clearance, moving from the course arrow to the bearing pointer and adding the intercept increment without hesitation. Closure was uniform, no heading required revision and the course was joined with deviations not exceeding 1 to 2 deg.
texts.marginal: SP built the inbound intercept headings from the bearing pointer correctly, but the increment was worked out only after the turn had started and one heading was refined in flight, leaving the deviation at about 4 deg when closure finally began. Accuracy is inside the standard while the heading is being produced late. SP is expected to read the course arrow, the bearing pointer and the intercept increment as one step before the turn.

texts_at.0: SP built inbound intercept headings with the IP talking through the course arrow, the bearing pointer and the increment as each heading was constructed. This is SP's first exposure to building the intercept heading from the bearing pointer, and the increment used has not yet been learned well enough to apply without help. The Training Section introduces this maneuver at this point and does not yet ask for an independent standard. SP is expected to begin constructing the heading independently from the course arrow and the bearing pointer, with the IP available to confirm the increment.
texts_at.1: SP built the inbound intercept heading to the standard expected at this stage, with the deviation reaching about 8 deg before the heading was corrected. The intercept angle was added only after the IP prompted with the heading to fly, because the 30 deg increment is still being estimated rather than built from the bearing pointer. Performance met the desired standard for this stage. SP is expected to construct the heading from the course arrow to the bearing pointer plus the increment as one step before the turn.
texts_at.2: SP built the inbound intercept heading correctly on every clearance without prompting, with the deviation reaching about 7 deg before the rebuilt heading closed the course. The 30 deg increment is still applied from an estimated bearing pointer position rather than the one actually displayed. This is consistent with the expected proficiency for the Training Section. SP is expected to read the bearing pointer position precisely before adding the increment rather than estimating it.
texts_at.3: SP built each inbound intercept heading from the course arrow to the bearing pointer plus 30 deg on three of the four intercepts, joining the course within 5 deg. The fourth needed a small revision once airborne, following a late read of the bearing pointer rather than any error in the construction. The result is in line with the proficiency expected at this point of the syllabus. SP is expected to read the bearing pointer as promptly on that intercept as on the other three.

texts_above.1: SP built the inbound intercept heading, holding the resulting deviation to about 8 deg, at the tolerance limit, before the heading was corrected. The correction followed a verbal call from the IP. Performance was above the level required at this point of the syllabus.
texts_above.2: SP built the inbound intercept heading correctly on every clearance without prompting, holding the deviation to about 7 deg before the rebuilt heading closed the course inside 5 deg. Reading the bearing pointer position precisely before adding the increment, rather than estimating it, would remove that rebuild. The result is above the code required for this Training Section, due to steady heading-construction technique.
texts_above.3: SP built each inbound intercept heading from the course arrow, up the case to the bearing pointer and 30 deg beyond it, flying that heading until the rollout so the assigned course was joined within 5 deg on every intercept. Performance was above the level required at this point of the syllabus, due to precise use of the bearing pointer.
texts_above.4: SP produced the inbound intercept heading immediately on each clearance, moving from the course arrow to the bearing pointer and adding the intercept increment without hesitation, joining the course with deviations not exceeding 1 to 2 deg. This is beyond what the Training Section asks for at this stage, due to first-rate geometric recall.

error_modes.label: OUTBOUND INTERCEPT HEADING AND THE 45 DEG INTERCEPT ANGLE

texts.0: SP, due to an outbound intercept heading that was not built from the tail of the bearing pointer to the course arrow and 45 deg beyond it, did not establish an angle capable of intercepting the outbound course. The heading flown diverged from the desired outbound course and the deviation ran beyond 8 deg and continued to grow. IP intervened and set the outbound intercept heading.
texts.1: SP, due to an outbound intercept angle reduced well below the 45 deg the technique recommends, did not obtain a usable rate of intercept on the outbound course. The CDI moved so slowly that the deviation held at 8 deg for the whole leg. SP increased the intercept angle only after the IP directed the heading to fly.
texts.2: SP, due to the 45 deg increment being applied from the tail of the bearing pointer instead of from the course arrow, did not build the outbound intercept heading as the technique describes. The angle was in error and the deviation reached 7 deg before the course began to close. SP rebuilt the heading from the course arrow and joined the outbound course within 5 deg without IP intervention.
texts.3: SP built each outbound intercept heading from the tail of the bearing pointer, up the case to the course arrow and 45 deg beyond it, having first set the desired outbound course. The rate of intercept was suitable and the outbound course was joined within 5 deg.
texts.4: SP set the desired outbound course and produced the intercept heading with the standard 45 deg angle without hesitation, adjusting it only where the rate of intercept desired called for it. Every outbound course was joined smoothly with deviations not exceeding 1 to 2 deg.
texts.marginal: SP used the standard 45 deg outbound intercept angle and joined the course inside the standard, but the angle was applied without regard to the displacement, so the small intercepts were flown at an unnecessarily high rate and closed with about 4 deg of overshoot. The result meets the standard while the angle is being used as a fixed value. SP is expected to start from 45 deg and adjust it to the rate of intercept desired.

texts_at.0: SP flew outbound intercepts with the IP setting the desired outbound course and talking through the standard intercept angle for each heading. This is SP's first exposure to building an outbound intercept heading from the tail of the bearing pointer, and applying the standard increment has not yet become routine. This is the level of assistance the Training Section still provides at this stage. SP is expected to begin building the outbound heading independently from the standard angle, with the IP available to confirm the rate of intercept.
texts_at.1: SP built the outbound intercept heading to the standard expected at this stage, with the deviation reaching about 8 deg before the angle was increased and the course closed. The intercept angle was raised only after the IP directed the heading to fly, because the 45 deg reference is still being reduced further than the technique intends. Performance met the desired standard for this stage. SP is expected to start from the standard 45 deg angle rather than reducing it before the rate of intercept desired calls for it.
texts_at.2: SP built the outbound intercept heading correctly on every clearance without prompting, with the deviation reaching about 7 deg before the rebuilt heading closed the course. The 45 deg increment is still applied from the tail of the bearing pointer rather than from the course arrow on one leg. This is consistent with the expected proficiency for the Training Section. SP is expected to build the increment from the course arrow on every outbound leg, not only most of them.
texts_at.3: SP built each outbound intercept heading from the tail of the bearing pointer to the course arrow plus 45 deg on three of the four legs, joining the course within 5 deg. The fourth leg used a slightly reduced angle for a small displacement without departing from the construction itself. The result is in line with the proficiency expected at this point of the syllabus. SP is expected to keep the increment at 45 deg as the starting point on every leg, adjusting only where the rate of intercept requires it.

texts_above.1: SP built the outbound intercept heading, holding the resulting deviation to about 8 deg, at the tolerance limit, before the angle was increased and the course closed. The correction followed a verbal call from the IP. This is beyond what the Training Section asks for at this stage of training.
texts_above.2: SP built the outbound intercept heading correctly on every clearance without prompting, holding the deviation to about 7 deg before the rebuilt heading closed the course inside 5 deg. Building the increment from the course arrow on every leg, rather than most of them, would remove that rebuild. The result is above the code required for this Training Section, due to assured outbound-heading construction.
texts_above.3: SP built each outbound intercept heading from the tail of the bearing pointer, up the case to the course arrow and 45 deg beyond it, having first set the desired outbound course, so the rate of intercept was suitable and the course was joined within 5 deg. Performance was above the level required at this point of the syllabus, due to well-developed outbound technique.
texts_above.4: SP set the desired outbound course and produced the intercept heading with the standard 45 deg angle without hesitation, adjusting it only where the rate of intercept desired called for it, joining every course smoothly with deviations not exceeding 1 to 2 deg. This is beyond what the Training Section asks for at this stage, due to exceptional rate-of-intercept judgment.

error_modes.label: DRIFT CORRECTION COMPUTED FROM CROSSWIND AND TRUE AIRSPEED

texts.0: SP, due to a drift correction that was never computed from the crosswind component and the true airspeed in NM per minute, did not correct for winds while maintaining the assigned course. The heading was held equal to the course, drift was allowed to run unopposed and the deviation passed 8 deg and continued to open. IP intervened and set the heading required to hold the course.
texts.1: SP, due to a drift correction guessed instead of derived from the crosswind component divided by the true airspeed in NM per minute, did not apply a correction that matched the wind. The correction was several degrees short of the drift and the deviation stabilized at the 8 deg limit. SP recomputed and applied an adequate correction only after the IP called the drift.
texts.2: SP, due to a crosswind component estimated from the forecast rather than from the wind actually observed, did not compute a drift correction adequate for the leg. The correction was undersized and the deviation reached 7 deg before it was noticed. SP recomputed the correction from the crosswind and the airspeed in NM per minute and regained the course inside 5 deg without IP intervention.
texts.3: SP computed the drift correction by dividing the crosswind component by the true airspeed in NM per minute and applied it as soon as the course was joined. The wind correction angle held the deviation within 5 deg on both the inbound and the outbound legs.
texts.4: SP computed the drift correction from the crosswind component and the true airspeed before joining the course and applied it at rollout, so that the CDI stayed centred from the start of the leg. The correction was refined by no more than 1 to 2 deg and the course was held with no visible needle movement.
texts.marginal: SP computed a drift correction from the crosswind component and the airspeed, but rounded it down and held the reduced value, so the course was maintained with a slow drift that reached about 4 deg before each additional correction. Accuracy stays inside the standard while the computed correction is not being applied in full. SP is expected to apply the correction obtained from the crosswind divided by the true airspeed in NM per minute and to refine it from the observed drift.

texts_at.0: SP flew the course with the IP computing the drift correction from the crosswind component and the true airspeed and talking through the arithmetic for each leg. This is SP's first exposure to dividing the crosswind component by the true airspeed in NM per minute, and applying the computed correction in full has not yet become routine. The maneuver is being introduced at this point of the syllabus, so no independent standard is required yet. SP is expected to begin computing the drift correction independently from the crosswind and the true airspeed, with the IP available to confirm the arithmetic.
texts_at.1: SP computed a drift correction to the standard expected at this stage, with the deviation reaching about 8 deg before an adequate correction was applied. The correction was recomputed only after the IP called the drift, because the crosswind component is still being estimated rather than derived from the true airspeed in NM per minute. Performance met the desired standard for this stage. SP is expected to divide the observed crosswind component by the true airspeed rather than estimating the correction directly.
texts_at.2: SP computed a workable drift correction on every leg without prompting, with the deviation reaching about 7 deg before the recomputed correction closed the course. The crosswind component is still taken from the forecast rather than the wind actually observed on one leg. This is consistent with the expected proficiency for the Training Section. SP is expected to base the crosswind component on the observed drift on every leg, not only most of them.
texts_at.3: SP computed the drift correction from the crosswind component and the true airspeed on three of the four legs, holding the deviation within 5 deg. The fourth needed a small refinement once the wind shifted, following the change rather than any error in the computation. The standard for the Training Section was met. SP is expected to refine the correction as promptly for a shifting wind as for a steady one.

texts_above.1: SP computed a drift correction, holding the resulting deviation to about 8 deg, at the tolerance limit, before an adequate correction was applied. The correction followed a verbal call from the IP. This is above the level the Training Section requires at this point.
texts_above.2: SP computed a workable drift correction on every leg without prompting, holding the deviation to about 7 deg before the recomputed correction closed the course inside 5 deg. Basing the crosswind component on the observed drift on every leg, rather than most, would remove that recomputation. The result is above the code required for this Training Section, due to competent drift computation.
texts_above.3: SP computed the drift correction by dividing the crosswind component by the true airspeed in NM per minute and applied it as soon as the course was joined, holding the deviation within 5 deg on both legs. Performance was above the level required at this point of the syllabus, due to disciplined wind-correction arithmetic.
texts_above.4: SP computed the drift correction from the crosswind component and the true airspeed before joining the course and applied it at rollout so the CDI stayed centred from the start of the leg, refined by no more than 1 to 2 deg. This is beyond what the Training Section asks for at this stage, due to superior wind-correction accuracy.

error_modes.label: MARKING THE INTERCEPT HEADING WITH THE HEADING BUG

texts.0: SP, due to an intercept heading that was never marked with the heading bug and was then lost while the navigation display was being worked, did not fly the heading computed for the intercept. The rollout was made on a heading far from the one required, the course was not closed and the deviation exceeded 8 deg. IP intervened and directed the intercept heading.
texts.1: SP, due to the heading bug being left where the previous leg had set it, did not have the computed intercept heading marked during the turn. The rollout was about 8 deg off the required heading, at the tolerance limit, and the deviation held there until the IP called the heading error. SP then flew the computed heading, but only after the prompt.
texts.2: SP, due to the heading bug being set only after the turn had been started, did not have the intercept heading marked at the moment of rollout. The rollout was about 6 deg off the computed heading and the deviation reached 7 deg before the error was seen. SP set the bug, corrected onto the computed heading and joined the course within 5 deg without IP intervention.
texts.3: SP marked the computed intercept heading with the heading bug before each turn and rolled out within 5 deg of it. The bug was reset for the next leg as the course was joined and no intercept heading had to be recalled from memory.
texts.4: SP set the heading bug on the computed intercept heading as part of the solution and rolled out on it within 2 deg on every intercept. The bug was moved to the wind corrected heading once the course was joined, so the reference on the case always matched the heading being flown.
texts.marginal: SP marked the intercept headings with the heading bug and held them inside the standard, but the bug was set as the bank was going in rather than before the turn, and one rollout finished about 4 deg off the computed heading. Performance meets the standard while the reference is still being set under time pressure. SP is expected to mark the intercept heading with the bug as soon as it is computed and before the turn is started.

texts_at.0: SP flew the intercepts with the IP marking the heading bug on the computed intercept heading and calling out the reference before each turn. This is SP's first exposure to marking the intercept heading with the bug as a distinct step, and setting it before the turn has not yet been built into the sequence. Performance is consistent with a first exposure at this point of the syllabus, where the Training Section still provides assistance. SP is expected to begin marking the bug independently as the heading is computed, with the IP available to confirm the reference.
texts_at.1: SP marked the intercept heading to the standard expected at this stage, with the rollout reaching about 8 deg off the computed heading before it was corrected. The bug was set only after the IP called the heading error, because the previous leg's setting is still being left on the bug into the next turn. Performance met the desired standard for this stage. SP is expected to reset the heading bug for the new intercept as soon as it is computed, before the turn begins.
texts_at.2: SP marked the computed intercept heading with the bug before most turns without prompting, with the rollout reaching about 7 deg off the computed heading once before the bug was set and the course closed. The bug is still being set after the turn has started on that leg rather than before it. This is consistent with the expected proficiency for the Training Section. SP is expected to set the bug before every turn, not only most of them.
texts_at.3: SP marked the computed intercept heading with the heading bug before three of the four turns, rolling out within 5 deg of it each time. The fourth turn had the bug set a moment into the roll rather than before it, without the rollout being affected. The result is in line with the proficiency expected at this point of the syllabus. SP is expected to set the bug before every turn so none are flown without the reference already in place.

texts_above.1: SP marked the intercept heading, holding the rollout to about 8 deg off the computed heading, at the tolerance limit for the stage, before it was corrected. The correction followed a verbal call from the IP. The result is above the code required for this Training Section at this stage of training.
texts_above.2: SP marked the computed intercept heading with the bug before most turns without prompting, holding the rollout from the one exception to about 7 deg off the computed heading before the course closed inside 5 deg. Setting the bug before every turn, rather than most of them, would remove that exception. The result is above the code required for this Training Section, due to steady use of the heading bug.
texts_above.3: SP marked the computed intercept heading with the heading bug before each turn and rolled out within 5 deg of it, resetting the bug for the next leg as the course was joined so no heading had to be recalled from memory. Performance was above the level required at this point of the syllabus, due to well-developed cockpit organization.
texts_above.4: SP set the heading bug on the computed intercept heading as part of the solution and rolled out on it within 2 deg on every intercept, moving it to the wind corrected heading once the course was joined so the reference always matched the heading flown. This is beyond what the Training Section asks for at this stage, due to exemplary reference management.
